title: Servant of God, well done
short: God's welcome to Abdiel plays on his name and on the master's praise in the parable of the talents; Verity suspects Milton thought of his own isolation.
body: Abdiel returns to Heaven expecting to bring news of the revolt and finds the angels already armed. The divine voice greets him: 'Servant of God, well done, well hast thou fought The better fight, who single hast maintaind Against revolted multitudes the Cause Of Truth'. 'Servant of God' translates his name, and 'well done' echoes the master's words to the faithful servant in the parable of the talents (Matthew 25:21), which also underlies Milton's sonnet on his blindness. Verity lists other texts glanced at, including 'I have fought a good fight' (2 Timothy 4:7), and asks whether Milton is thinking of himself, who bore reproach for the republican cause when 'revolted multitudes' welcomed the Restoration. The praise also implies that bearing witness matters more than victory: Abdiel was 'judg'd perverse' by the many.

title: Michael of Celestial Armies Prince; Gabriel
short: Michael leads the loyal angels, as in Revelation 12, where he fights the dragon; Gabriel is second in command.
body: The Father sends Michael and Gabriel to drive the rebels out. Michael's name is a question, 'Who is like God?', the perfect rebuke to a rebel who aspired to be God's equal; Verity gives the meaning and quotes Christian Doctrine 1.9, where Milton identifies Michael as the leader of the good angels on the basis of Revelation 12:7-9 ('Michael and his angels fought against the dragon') and Daniel 12:1 ('Michael ... the great prince'). Gabriel is 'next' in rank (see 4.549). A notable feature of the poem is that Michael does not win the war: after two days of indecisive fighting the Father sends the Son, so the victory of Revelation 12 is transferred to the Messiah. Michael returns in Books XI-XII as the messenger who expels Adam and Eve and shows Adam the future.

title: This is servitude, To serve th' unwise
short: Abdiel's definition of true slavery: not serving God, who is worthiest, but serving the unworthy or being enslaved to oneself.
body: Satan taunts Abdiel as a servile angel who prefers 'Ministring Spirits' to freedom. Abdiel replies that 'Unjustly thou deprav'st it with the name Of servitude to serve whom God ordains, Or Nature; God and Nature bid the same, When he who rules is worthiest'. 'This is servitude, To serve th' unwise, or him who hath rebelld Against his worthier, as thine now serve thee, Thy self not free, but to thy self enthrall'd'. Verity compares Horace's Stoic argument that the man ruled by his passions is a slave (Satires 2.7.80-82), and notes that Abdiel's 'Reign thou in Hell thy Kingdom' answers Satan's 'Better to reign in Hell' (1.263). The passage is central to Milton's political thought: liberty means obedience to right reason and worth, not mere absence of rule, a view he restates in Michael's account of tyranny (12.79-101).

title: Satan first knew pain: the sword of Michael and the 'Nectarous humor'
short: Michael's sword, tempered in 'the Armorie of God', shears through Satan's side; he feels pain for the first time and bleeds a heavenly fluid like Homer's ichor.
body: Michael's sword, given him 'from the Armorie of God' (Jeremiah 50:25, 'The Lord hath opened his armoury'), cuts Satan's sword in two and shears through his right side: 'then Satan first knew pain'. The wound closes at once, 'so sore The griding sword with discontinuous wound Pass'd through him, but th' Ethereal substance clos'd Not long divisible'. Verity explains 'discontinuous' from the old medical definition of a wound as a breach of continuity, and notes that only the rebels feel pain, because sin has coarsened their substance (6.660-61, 691). From the wound flows 'A stream of Nectarous humor', which recalls Homer's ichor, the fluid that flows from wounded gods (Iliad 5.339-42, where Diomedes wounds Aphrodite); Verity records Bentley's proposal to read 'ichorous'. The scene partly echoes the wounding of gods in Homeric battle.

title: Adramelec and Asmadai
short: Two rebel 'Thrones' named after later false gods: the Sepharvite god Adrammelech, to whom children were burned, and Asmodeus of Tobit.
body: Uriel and Raphael defeat 'Adramelec, and Asmadai, Two potent Thrones, that to be less then Gods Disdain'd'. As in the catalogue of Book I, the rebels bear the names of gods later worshipped by men. Adrammelech was a god of the colonists from Sepharvaim settled in Samaria, to whom 'the Sepharvites burnt their children in fire' (2 Kings 17:31); Verity glosses the name as 'magnificence of the king' and the Dartmouth edition as 'mighty king'. Asmadai is Asmodeus, the demon of Tobit (see 4.168); Verity shows from Heywood's Hierarchy, Reginald Scot and the Faust-book that demonology made him a mighty king among devils, which gives point to his defeat here. Note the deflating irony: these 'Thrones' who scorned to be less than gods flee 'Mangl'd with gastly wounds'.

title: Ariel, Arioc, and Ramiel
short: Three rebels overthrown by Abdiel, with names chosen for their meaning and sound rather than from any biblical list of angels.
body: Abdiel 'Ariel and Arioc, and the violence Of Ramiel scorcht and blasted overthrew'. Verity explains the names: Ariel, 'lion of God', a title of Jerusalem in Isaiah 29:1 and a man's name in Ezra 8:16; Arioch, 'lion-like', a king in Genesis 14:1 and Nebuchadnezzar's captain in Daniel 2:14, whom Nashe's Pierce Penniless calls 'the spirit of revenge'; and Ramiel, whose source Verity does not know, though the Dartmouth edition identifies a Ramiel among the fallen 'watchers' of the apocryphal Book of Enoch. Verity quotes Tennyson's remark that Milton's proper names are often chosen for their full sound. The line shows Milton's habit of making catalogues out of resonant names, and it is apt that the 'servant of God' should overthrow the 'lions'.

title: Nisroc, of Principalities the prime
short: The rebel who, after the first day's fighting, admits that pain is the worst misery and that without exemption from it they cannot win.
body: Nisroch was the Assyrian god in whose temple Sennacherib was murdered by his sons (2 Kings 19:37; Isaiah 37:38); Verity gives the references and suggests the name may mean 'great eagle'. In the council of the first night Nisroc, bruised and hacked, speaks frankly: they cannot fight on equal terms against those who feel no pain, for 'Sense of pleasure we may well Spare out of life perhaps, and not repine, But live content ... but pain is perfet miserie, the worst Of evils' (6.459-63). Verity notes that his complaint, against those 'impassive', points to the rebels' new vulnerability. Satan answers by revealing his invention: if their swords are unequal, they will find stronger weapons, and so artillery enters Heaven.

title: devilish Engins: the invention of artillery
short: Satan invents gunpowder and cannon on the second day of the war, following a Renaissance commonplace that firearms were a devilish invention.
body: Satan proposes to dig 'materials dark and crude' from the soil of Heaven, nitre and sulphur, and to ram them into 'hallow Engins long and round' (cannon) fired by an 'incentive reed' (the match). Verity notes that the idea that cannon were invented in Hell appears in Ariosto (Orlando Furioso 9.28-29), Spenser (Faerie Queene 1.7.13) and Drayton; Raphael adds that some future son of Adam, 'bent on mischief', may invent them again (6.501-06), which Verity takes as an allusion to the Civil War. The guns knock the loyal angels over in heaps, and the scene is often read as deliberate absurdity: Satan's ingenuity produces only 'devilish Enginrie' and puns. Raphael's warning that he speaks 'By lik'ning spiritual to corporal forms' (5.573) is relevant to how literally to take it.

title: So they among themselves in pleasant veine Stood scoffing
short: Satan and Belial mock the fallen loyal angels with puns on 'overture', 'terms' and 'understand'; the jokes are a deliberate study in devilish wit.
body: When the cannon knock over the loyal angels, Satan and Belial exchange jests: Satan pretends they had offered 'composition' and 'overture' (peace terms, and the gun-muzzles' openings) which the foe received oddly; Belial replies that their 'terms of weight' 'stumble many' and that whoever receives them must 'understand' (stand under) them (6.609-27). Verity observes that the speeches are 'full of obvious quibbles', and quotes Newton and Addison that the speech fits Belial, celebrated in battle 'for nothing but that scoffing speech'. The Dartmouth edition notes that the loyal angels never answer scorn with scorn. Readers from Johnson onward have disliked the puns; others take them as Milton's deliberate demonstration that wit without truth is cheap, a fitting contrast to the 'grand pause' of the Son's advent.

title: They pluckt the seated Hills ... Hills amid the Air encounterd Hills
short: The loyal angels tear up the hills of Heaven and hurl them on the cannon; the rebels reply in kind, recalling the Giants who piled Ossa on Pelion.
body: Inspired by fury, the loyal angels throw away their arms and pluck up the hills 'with all thir load, Rocks, Waters, Woods', bury the artillery under them, and the rebels answer with hills of their own until 'Hills amid the Air encounterd Hills'. Verity notes Addison's comparison with the Giants' war against the gods, in which the giants Otus and Ephialtes piled Mount Ossa on Olympus and Pelion on Ossa to scale heaven (Odyssey 11.313-16; Virgil, Georgics 1.281-83); he also cites Virgil's 'furor arma ministrat' (Aeneid 1.150), 'rage supplies arms'. Here the good angels play the giants' role, which complicates the classical identification of the rebels with the Titans. The escalation threatens the fabric of Heaven itself (6.669-70), and the Father ends the war on the third day.

title: the third sacred Morn
short: The Son ends the war on the third day, a deliberate foreshadowing of the resurrection on the third day.
body: After two days of indecisive fighting the Father declares that the Son alone shall end the war, so that all may know 'that thou art worthiest to be Heir' (6.707-08). 'The third sacred Morn began to shine' as he goes out. Verity quotes Newton: by continuing the war for three days and reserving the victory on the third for the Messiah, Milton plainly alludes to the death and resurrection; the Dartmouth edition cites Matthew 16:21, 'be raised again the third day'. Verity adds that schoolmen had debated the length of the angelic war, and that Revelation 12 gives the victory to Michael, so Milton's choice is deliberate: the first defeat of Satan prefigures the final one, which makes Paradise Lost and Paradise Regained a single action.

title: The Chariot of Paternal Deitie
short: The Son rides out in the Father's chariot, drawn from Ezekiel's vision of the four living creatures and the wheels within wheels.
body: The chariot comes 'Flashing thick flames, Wheele within Wheele', 'convoyd By four Cherubic shapes, four Faces each', with bodies and wings set with eyes, above them 'a Saphir Throne'. Every detail is from Ezekiel's visions of God's throne-chariot (Ezekiel 1:4-28 and 10:9-19), as the Dartmouth edition notes; Jewish mystics called this the merkavah. Verity adds that the Son rides 'Sublime' on the cherub as in Psalm 18:10 ('he rode upon a cherub, and did fly'), and that 'Ten thousand thousand Saints' attend him (Jude 14; Daniel 7:10). The Dartmouth edition also observes a classical contrast: unlike Phaethon, who stole his father's sun-chariot and nearly burned the world (Ovid, Metamorphoses 2), the Son is invited to drive it. Milton later used the 'chariot of paternal deity' as the vehicle of creation (7.197-209).

title: radiant Urim
short: The Son's armour shines with Urim, the mysterious objects in the high priest's breastplate through which God's will was revealed.
body: The Son is 'in Celestial Panoplie all armd Of radiant Urim, work divinely wrought'. 'Panoply' recalls 'the whole armour of God' (Ephesians 6:11), as Verity notes. The Urim, with the Thummim, were placed in the breastplate of judgment worn by the high priest (Exodus 28:30) and were used to learn God's will. Verity sets out the debated theories of what they were, gems, inscribed lots or small images, and says that Milton, here and in Paradise Regained (3.13-15), takes them to be precious stones; Tennyson followed him in describing 'elfin Urim' on the hilt of Excalibur. Milton connects the radiance of the Son's armour with oracular light: the Son's appearance is itself the revelation of God's judgment.

title: Nine dayes they fell; confounded Chaos roard
short: The rebels, driven over the wall of Heaven, fall for nine days through Chaos into Hell, as the Titans fell nine days to Tartarus.
body: Driven by the Son's thunder to the edge of Heaven, which opens 'wide, Rowling in a spacious Gap', the rebels throw themselves down: 'Nine dayes they fell; confounded Chaos roard, And felt tenfold confusion in thir fall'. The Dartmouth edition traces the nine days to Hesiod's Titans, who would fall nine days and nights from heaven (Theogony 720-25); Verity recalls that nine was a significant number and cross-refers to 1.50, where the rebels then lie nine days on the burning lake. 'Hell at last Yawning receavd them whole' echoes Isaiah 5:14, 'hell hath enlarged herself, and opened her mouth without measure', which Verity cites. Chaos, which Satan will later cross, reports the event to him at 2.993-98. Raphael's narrative thus reaches the point at which the poem began.

title: remember, and fear to transgress
short: Raphael ends his war story with its moral for Adam: the rebels fell though great; let Adam warn 'thy weaker', Eve.
body: Raphael closes with the purpose of his narrative: Satan envies Adam's state and plots to seduce him; 'let it profit thee to have heard By terrible Example the reward Of disobedience'. He adds 'warn Thy weaker', which Verity glosses from 1 Peter 3:7, where the wife is 'the weaker vessel'. The final line, 'Yet fell; remember, and fear to transgress', ends the book with a monosyllabic warning. The structural point is that the war in Heaven, though it occupies the centre of the poem, is told as an exemplum, a cautionary tale with a lesson; whether Raphael's account succeeds as a warning, given that Adam later falls 'not deceav'd' (9.998), is part of the poem's long argument about knowledge and obedience.
